title: Why does a nickel cost 13 cents to make?

record.question: Why does a nickel cost 13 cents to make, and why does the Mint keep making it?
record.audience_reason: Everyone handles nickels; the penny just ended and Congress is now changing the nickel. Recognizable in the news and at the register.

editorial_contribution.statement: We follow one coin through the Mint's own FY2025 cost lines (10.97 + 2.24 + 0.10 = 13.31 cents), show it sold to the Fed at face value, scale the gap to the year's 615 million coins, and resolve why the Mint can't simply switch metals (the alloy is in the statute).

record.custom_scene: A single nickel rides a production line under a running cost meter; a to-scale receipt bar with a face-value line; a coin-and-5¢ exchange with the Fed; a growing coin pile with a shortfall counter; cross-sections of today's alloy vs the bill's zinc core.

cover_composition.main_object: a single nickel, huge, with a 13.31¢ tag

record.sources_and_assumptions: See sources-and-rights.md. Assumptions: the Mint's unit cost includes cost of goods sold, SG&A and distribution to the Fed; the report does not split metal from fabrication, so the script says 'metal plus making'. Bill status: passed by Congress Sept 2026; the script says 'would let Treasury test', which holds whether or not it has been signed.

scenes.subject: one nickel, huge, with WORTH 5¢ and COST TO MAKE 13.31¢ tags
changes: 0.0s coin spinning, both tags on (matches cover)
cost tag pulses on 'more than thirteen'

explain.understand: the coin costs more than it is worth
explain.change: cost tag appears beside the face value

scenes.tts: This coin is worth five cents. Making it and shipping it cost the U.S. Mint more than thirteen.
scenes.caption: This coin is worth five cents.|Making it and shipping it|cost the U.S. Mint more than thirteen.

scenes.subject: a cupronickel strip, the recipe card, the press punching a blank; meter climbs to 10.97¢

explain.understand: most of the cost is metal and manufacturing, and the metal mix is fixed by law
explain.change: meter climbs as the coin is made

scenes.tts: Follow one nickel. It starts as a strip of metal: three parts copper, one part nickel, a recipe set by federal law. A press punches out a blank and stamps it. Metal plus making: about eleven cents.
scenes.caption: Follow one nickel.|It starts as a strip of metal:|three parts copper, one part nickel,|a recipe set by federal law.|A press punches out a blank and stamps it.|Metal plus making: about eleven cents.

scenes.subject: the coin continues past the admin desk; meter +2.24¢

explain.understand: overhead adds a second, smaller slice
explain.cause: the coin's share of administrative costs

scenes.tts: Then its share of the Mint's admin costs. Another two and a quarter cents.
scenes.caption: Then its share of the Mint's admin costs.|Another two and a quarter cents.

scenes.subject: truck carries the coin to the Federal Reserve; total 13.31¢; to-scale receipt bar with a face-value line
changes: to-scale bar grows past the 5¢ line

explain.understand: the three slices add to 13.31¢, about 2.7 times the face value, shown to scale

scenes.tts: Shipping to the Fed adds a tenth of a cent. Total: thirteen point three one cents, the Mint's own figure for fiscal 2025.
scenes.caption: Shipping to the Fed adds a tenth of a cent.|Total: 13.31 cents,|the Mint's own figure for fiscal 2025.

scenes.subject: Mint and Fed exchange: coin goes right, 5¢ comes back, red 8.31¢ gap

explain.understand: the Mint is paid face value, so 8.31¢ per coin is uncovered
explain.change: the recovered part fills only 5 of 13.31

scenes.tts: Here's the catch. The Mint sells new coins to the Fed at face value. It gets five cents back... and swallows the rest.
scenes.caption: Here's the catch.|The Mint sells new coins to the Fed at face value.|It gets five cents back...|and swallows the rest.

scenes.subject: a pile of nickels grows; counters to 615 million and −$50.9 million
changes: pile grows and counter runs to 615 million

explain.understand: the per-coin gap becomes a $50.9 million yearly shortfall
explain.cause: 615 million coins × the per-coin gap (as reported)
text: ≈ −$1.64 for every $1 of nickels (on screen only)

scenes.tts: Last fiscal year, it shipped about 615 million nickels and came out almost 51 million dollars behind.
scenes.caption: Last fiscal year, it shipped about 615 million nickels|and came out almost 51 million dollars behind.

scenes.subject: penny struck out; cross-section of today's solid alloy vs the bill's zinc core with nickel outer layer
changes: zinc-core section and labels on 'zinc core'

explain.understand: the Mint can't change the metal by itself; the law is changing

scenes.tts: So why not stop, like the penny? Cash still needs a five-cent coin. And the Mint can't just switch metals: the recipe is in the law. In September, Congress passed a bill that would let Treasury test a zinc core with a nickel outer layer.
scenes.caption: So why not stop, like the penny?|Cash still needs a five-cent coin.|And the Mint can't just switch metals:|the recipe is in the law.|In September, Congress passed a bill|that would let Treasury test a zinc core|with a nickel outer layer.

scenes.subject: a paper receipt prints: face value 5¢, cost to make 13.31¢
scenes.tts: So every new nickel comes with an invisible receipt. Five cents of money. Thirteen cents of making. Follow for one bonus braincell per scroll.
scenes.caption: So every new nickel comes with an invisible receipt.|Five cents of money.|Thirteen cents of making.|Follow for one bonus braincell per scroll.
